1-1-15-write-a-task-set.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.1.12 (Software Engineering Actions), 1.1.13 (Task Sets) and the worked example in 1.1.14: go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words are fine.

A software engineering action is a named job inside a phase, and a task set is all the tasks required to accomplish one action.

Consider the action "requirements definition", which lives in the inception phase. List at least two tasks that would make up a task set for that action.

Each task should be a concrete step that "requirements definition" would actually need, for example interviewing users, writing a requirements document, or reviewing requirements with stakeholders. Other reasonable tasks are fine too.

rubric.title: At least two concrete tasks listed
rubric.description: Student lists at least two tasks for the 'requirements definition' action. Each task should be a concrete-ish step (e.g. interviewing users, writing a requirements document, reviewing requirements) rather than just restating the action itself. Be generous about what counts as concrete - a short, plausible step in the student's own words is enough, it doesn't need much detail. Full credit for two or more such tasks. If only one is concrete and the other just restates the action, credit as partial rather than missing; only fully withhold if fewer than two tasks are listed at all, or none rises above restating the action.

rubric.title: Tasks plausibly belong to requirements definition
rubric.description: Each listed task is plausibly something 'requirements definition' would need: interviewing stakeholders, documenting needs, reviewing requirements, and similar. Be generous - the rubric must NOT require an exact match to any specific examples, and the book explicitly allows 'other reasonable tasks.' Full credit if the tasks are all at least plausibly in the neighborhood. Only withhold credit if a task is clearly unrelated to figuring out what the software should do.

1-1-22-a1-2-describe-lifecycle.prompt:
Everything you need is in the 1.1.5 video, 1.1.6 (The Four Phases), the worked example in 1.1.8, and 1.1.10 (Umbrella Activities): go back and reread or rewatch if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout.

Part 1: Describe the four framework activities: inception, elaboration, construction and deployment. One or two sentences each about what happens in that activity. (1.1.5 and 1.1.6)

Part 2: Pick one real software product you actually use: Instagram, Spotify, Google Maps, Roblox, YouTube, Google Docs, anything. Name it, then walk it through all four activities, saying what you think happened in each one for that product. Best-guess reasoning is fine; no research needed. (1.1.8 shows this done for a greeting app)

Part 3: Name at least one umbrella activity, and say in one sentence why it runs across all four phases instead of sitting inside one of them. (1.1.10)

Part 4: Two namings, one lifecycle. The 1.1.5 video counts five phases (design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance); 1.1.6 counts four framework activities. They describe the same lifecycle. Name the two phases the four-activity list does not give a name of its own to, and say in one sentence each where that work happens in the four-activity view. (1.1.6, the table on this page)

rubric.title: All four phases named and described
rubric.description: Student names and describes all four framework activities: inception, elaboration, construction, deployment. Credit is generous per phase - a brief, even one-phrase description is enough, it doesn't need to be precise or complete. Full credit for all four named with some description, however short. If one of the four is missing entirely or named with no description at all, treat it as partial rather than denying the whole criterion.

rubric.title: One named real product
rubric.description: Student names one real software product they use (e.g. a specific app, game, or service). Any recognizable name counts, spelled however the student spells it. Credit generously; withhold credit only if no actual name appears anywhere (just 'an app' or 'a website' with nothing more specific).

rubric.title: One concrete sentence per phase for that product
rubric.description: Student gives at least one concrete sentence per phase for the named product, saying what probably happened in that phase for it. Credit a sentence as concrete even if it's a rough guess or thin - the point is that it's actually about the named product, not phase-content accuracy. Full credit for all four phases covered. If one phase is thin or missing while the other three are solid, treat it as partial rather than denying the whole criterion.

rubric.title: At least one umbrella activity mentioned by name
rubric.description: Student mentions at least one umbrella activity, even paraphrased rather than the exact course term (e.g. quality management, security management, risk management, configuration management, architecture management, training/communication). A close variant like 'security' or 'making sure it works well throughout' counts if it clearly points at one of these. Credit generously; withhold only if nothing resembling an umbrella activity appears anywhere.

rubric.title: Own words
rubric.description: The response is written in the student's own words, not copied from a source. Withhold credit only for significant issues: text that reads as copied/dictionary-style, or writing too disorganized to follow. Do not withhold for length: a short response that clearly covers the four phases and a product walkthrough is fine. This is not a prose-quality score.

rubric.title: Maps the four activities onto the five-phase naming
rubric.description: Student identifies testing and maintenance as the two phases the four-activity list does not name separately, and says roughly where each one lives - testing running across the phases (or inside construction), maintenance continuing after deployment. Credit naming both with any reasonable placement, even a vague one. Naming both but placing only one still earns it. Credit only one of the two named as partial rather than missing.

1-2-21-null-vs-undefined.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.2.19 (The null Value) and 1.2.20 (The undefined Value): go back and reread them if you get stuck. One or two sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Both null and undefined mean a variable has no useful value in it. They are not the same thing.

1. What does undefined mean, and who puts it there: you, or JavaScript? (1.2.20)

2. What does null mean, and who puts it there? (1.2.19)

3. Give one situation where you would write null yourself. Describe the variable and why null is the right value for it at that moment. (1.2.19)

4. A program prints undefined where you expected a name. What does that tell you about where the bug is? (1.2.20)

rubric.title: Q1: undefined means no value assigned, and JavaScript supplies it
rubric.description: Student says undefined means the variable was declared but never given a value, and that JavaScript sets it automatically rather than the programmer. Credit a loose or brief gesture at both ideas - 'JS puts that there automatically when nothing's assigned' covers both halves even said in passing. If only one half is clearly present, credit it as partial rather than treating the answer as missing.

rubric.title: Q2: null means deliberately empty, and the programmer writes it
rubric.description: Student says null means nothing / empty / value unknown, and that the programmer assigns it on purpose. Credit a loose or brief gesture at both ideas - describing null as something you set on purpose, even without the word 'deliberate', is enough. Give partial credit if only one half is clearly present. But do not credit an answer that describes null as only 'empty' with no sense that anyone chose it - that erases the one distinction between null and undefined this pair of questions is actually testing.

rubric.title: Q3: a concrete situation for writing null
rubric.description: Student describes a specific variable and moment - a chosen colour before the user picks one, a middle name that does not exist, a score before the game starts - and says why null fits. It does not need to be polished or original; any concrete, named situation counts, even a simple or slightly awkward one. A fully generic non-answer like 'when you want it to be empty' with no actual situation named does not give the grader anything to check, so that is the one thing to hold the line on.

rubric.title: Q4: infers that a value was never assigned
rubric.description: Student concludes that seeing undefined means the variable never got a value - the assignment did not happen, ran too late, or the wrong name was used - so the bug is upstream of the line that printed it. Credit any answer that connects undefined to 'the value was never set' in some form, even loosely phrased. An answer that only says 'there's a bug' with nothing about what undefined itself tells you has not shown the inference this question is checking for, so that one stays a miss.

rubric.title: All six names are judged
rubric.description: Student gives a verdict on each of the six names, and the verdicts broadly land in the expected place: x bad, numberOfStudents good, d bad, currentDay good, temp borderline-or-weak, bodyTemperature good. Credit any answer that addresses all six, even if a call or two beyond temp is debatable rather than a clean match - the point is that they engaged with each name and reasoned through most of them, not that every verdict landed exactly right.

rubric.title: Reasons name the rule, not just the verdict
rubric.description: For the bad names the student gives some reason grounded in the module's vocabulary - a single letter carries no information, the name is too vague, you can't tell what it holds, or something in that spirit even loosely phrased. Deny only bare verdicts ('bad', 'good') with literally no reason given, or 'it is confusing' repeated with nothing else attached.

rubric.title: Q7: identifies temp as the borderline one, with an argument
rubric.description: Student names temp and gives some reason it is arguable rather than simply bad - that it is a common short form, that it could be read more than one way, that experienced programmers would recognise it. Any real reason counts, however informally put. Credit naming temp with a reason; do not require them to weigh it against bodyTemperature.

rubric.title: Q8: the four problems are matched correctly
rubric.description: Expected matching: temp = too generic; x = abbreviation with no context; a1 = numbered name that says nothing; myVariable = meaningless but harmless-sounding. Accept any phrasing that captures the same idea, even loosely worded. Credit three or four correct; two or fewer is a genuine miss on the matching itself, not just phrasing.

1-3-17-team-vocabulary.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.3.9 (Agree on Terms): go back and reread it if you get stuck. Two or three sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

You have joined a team building an online shop.

1. The team calls a logged-in person a "member". Which variable name is better, currentMember or currentPerson? Say which, and why. (1.3.9)

2. Your team calls a shopping cart a "basket". A teammate's existing code uses cartItems. Your new code uses basketItems. What problem does that create for anyone reading the code, and what should you do about it? (1.3.9)

3. Suppose you genuinely prefer the word "cart", and the team has settled on "basket". What do you do, and why? Be honest about your reasoning.

rubric.title: Q1: picks currentMember and ties it to the team's word
rubric.description: Student chooses currentMember and explains that it matches the term the team already uses, keeping the vocabulary consistent. The reasoning can be brief or informally worded - 'because that's what the team calls it' is enough. If currentPerson is picked instead, or currentMember is picked with no reasoning at all, that misses the actual idea being tested - consistency with the team's vocabulary - so do not credit it.

rubric.title: Q2: names the reader's problem
rubric.description: Student identifies that a reader cannot tell whether cartItems and basketItems are two different things or the same thing under two names, or otherwise names the confusion/searchability cost of mixed vocabulary. Credit any answer that gestures at this cost, even briefly or in different words - 'someone reading it might think there are two carts' is enough. An answer that only says it is 'messy' or 'inconsistent' with no sense of what that actually costs a reader has not quite shown the idea yet, so treat that as partial rather than full credit.

rubric.title: Q2: says what to do
rubric.description: Student proposes an actual action - rename to match the existing code, or agree one term with the team and change everything to it. Credit either direction as long as the outcome is one word used everywhere, and be generous about how the action is described. An answer that says to leave it as-is, or that names no action at all, has not actually answered what the question asked, so that one does not earn credit.

rubric.title: Q3: consistency beats personal preference
rubric.description: Student says they would use the team's word despite preferring their own, and gives a reason grounded in the codebase - one word per idea is easier to read and search, and mixed vocabulary costs everyone. Be generous about how that reasoning is phrased; it does not need to be polished. If the student says they would keep using their own preferred word anyway, that answers a different question than the one being asked, so do not credit it. A reason that is purely social ('to be polite', 'to follow the rules') with no sense of why consistency actually helps the code is thinner - treat that as partial rather than full credit rather than a hard miss.

1-4-14-three-structures-three-examples.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.4.9 (Structured Programming), 1.4.10 (the three structures) and 1.4.13 (Why goto Went Away): go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words are fine.

1. Name the three structures that structured programming says every program can be built from. (1.4.9 and 1.4.10)

2. For each one, give a one-sentence example from ordinary life, not from code. Making toast, getting to school, a game you play, a chore you do. The example should make it obvious which structure it is. (1.4.10)

3. Structured programming also forbids arbitrary jumps between parts of a program. In one or two sentences, why was giving that up worth it? (1.4.13)

rubric.title: All three structures are named
rubric.description: Student names sequence, selection and repetition. Accept close synonyms freely - 'choice', 'branching', or 'if/else' for selection; 'loop', 'iteration', or 'repeat' for repetition; even 'in order' or 'one after another' for sequence. Full credit needs all three named, even loosely. Naming two of the three is partial credit rather than a miss; naming only one or none is where this criterion is genuinely not met.

rubric.title: Each example comes from ordinary life
rubric.description: All three examples are drawn from everyday activity rather than code. Be generous about how everyday or how simply stated the examples are - plain, ordinary examples are exactly what is being asked for. If the student illustrates a structure with actual code (an if statement, a for loop) instead of a real-world situation, that answers a different question than the one asked, so do not credit that example. Three solid everyday examples is full credit; two out of three is partial rather than missing - the count itself is part of what this question checks, since the assignment explicitly asks for three.

rubric.title: Each example actually matches its structure
rubric.description: The sequence example is genuinely steps in order; the selection example genuinely involves choosing between paths based on a condition; the repetition example genuinely involves doing something more than once. Be generous about how directly the example demonstrates this - it does not need to be a textbook case, just recognizably the right shape. If an example is actually mismatched, though - a plain list of steps offered as the repetition example, say - that shows the difference between the structures has not landed yet, which is the actual point of this question, so that one example does not earn credit even if the others do.

rubric.title: Explains why forbidding arbitrary jumps was worth it
rubric.description: Student says something about being able to follow or reason about the program - that you can tell how execution reached a line, that code becomes readable, that it prevents tangled flow. Credit any answer that connects the restriction to something it actually enables, even loosely or briefly phrased - 'so you can follow what's happening' is enough. An answer that only asserts it is 'better' or 'cleaner' with nothing about what that betterness consists of has not quite gotten there, so treat that as partial rather than full credit.

1-4-23-a1-4-1-two-languages.prompt:
1.4.2 and the 1.4.21 video cover why languages are built for different jobs; 1.4.7, 1.4.8, 1.4.15, 1.4.18 and 1.4.19 cover the paradigms. Go back and reread or rewatch if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout: do not copy descriptions from the internet, and you are not expected to have written code in either language.

Pick two programming languages other than JavaScript. 1.4.2 lists several, and you may pick others.

For each of your two languages, answer all three:
1. What is this language typically used for? Name a specific kind of software, not just "programs". (1.4.2)
2. Which paradigm or paradigms does it support: procedural, object-oriented, functional? You may name more than one. (1.4.7 and 1.4.19)
3. Why does that paradigm suit that kind of work? This is the important part. Connect the way the language organises a solution to the kind of problem it is usually pointed at. (1.4.8, 1.4.15 and 1.4.18)

Then close with one sentence: name one thing that would make you pick a different language than either of these for a job.

rubric.title: Two specific non-JavaScript languages are named
rubric.description: Student names two distinct, real programming languages, neither of which is JavaScript. HTML and CSS do not count as programming languages and don't earn this criterion on their own; SQL does count. Credit any real language named clearly enough to identify - a common nickname or informal name is fine. Only withhold credit if just one language is actually discussed, or if a 'language' named is so vague it can't be identified as any real one ('a systems language').

rubric.title: Each language's typical use is specific
rubric.description: For both languages the student names a concrete-ish kind of software or task - 'analysing data sets', 'iPhone apps', 'operating systems', 'querying a database'. Be generous about what counts as concrete: a plausible, recognizable use case in the student's own words is enough, even if broad ('building websites' counts). Credit both when covered; if one language's use is specific and the other is generic filler ('making programs', 'websites and stuff'), credit it as partial rather than missing.

rubric.title: A paradigm is named for each language
rubric.description: For both languages the student names at least one paradigm from the course vocabulary - procedural, object-oriented, or functional - and the pairing is defensible. Credit a reasonable pairing generously, even if incomplete or imprecisely worded (e.g. calling Python object-oriented without also saying it is multi-paradigm). If a paradigm is missing for one language but present and reasonable for the other, credit as partial rather than missing. Only withhold full credit where a pairing is plainly wrong (e.g. 'SQL is object-oriented').

rubric.title: The fit between paradigm and purpose is explained, not just asserted
rubric.description: This is the core of the assignment. For at least one language, the student gives a reason connecting the paradigm to the kind of work - for example that a database question is declarative because you want rows back and don't care how they're found, or that game and app code suits objects because there are many similar things each keeping their own state. Be generous about how the reasoning is worded - a rough, intuitive version of the connection counts, it doesn't need textbook precision. Only withhold credit if the answer purely asserts the pairing with nothing at all connecting it to the kind of work ('Python is object-oriented and that fits data science').

rubric.title: Written in the student's own words
rubric.description: The writing reads as a beginner's own understanding, with personal phrasing and natural variation. Be generous - uneven or clunky phrasing is expected and fine. Only withhold credit if it clearly reads as copied marketing copy or encyclopedia text: polished, uniform, and using terminology well beyond anything else in the submission.

1-5-17-a1-5-2-computational-thinking.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.5.3 (What Computational Thinking Is) and 1.5.4 (The Four Cornerstones), with 1.5.8, 1.5.9 and 1.5.13 covering the individual parts: go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout; do not copy definitions from the internet.

Part 1: The four parts. For each one below, write one or two sentences saying what it means: (1.5.4)
1. Decomposition: breaking a big problem into smaller pieces you can handle one at a time (1.5.8)
2. Pattern recognition: noticing where those pieces repeat, or resemble something you have solved before (1.5.9)
3. Abstraction: ignoring the details that do not matter for the problem you are solving (1.5.13)
4. Algorithmic thinking: putting the pieces into a precise sequence of steps someone else could follow (1.5.4)

Part 2: One example each. Give one concrete example of each of the four, drawn from one program you have actually written this quarter: a lab from module 1.2 or 1.3. If you truly cannot find all four in one program, an everyday task is accepted instead, but try the code first. Name the task, then say what the decomposition, the pattern, the abstraction and the algorithm were in that specific case. (1.5.15 shows this done for a game of chess)

rubric.title: All four parts explained
rubric.description: Student addresses all four of decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking in Part 1, each by name (or an unmistakable synonym) and each with some explanation, however brief or informally worded. Credit any answer that touches all four, even lightly - the point is that they engaged with each term, not that each explanation is polished or lengthy.

rubric.title: Explanations are in the student's own words
rubric.description: The definitions read as a beginner's own understanding rather than copied text. Look for personal phrasing and natural variation. Deny if the wording matches dictionary or textbook definitions verbatim.

rubric.title: A specific task is named in Part 2
rubric.description: Student names one concrete thing they actually did, however briefly - a specific program or lab from this quarter ('the ten broken declarations lab', 'my object description') or a specific everyday activity. Any real named thing counts, even mentioned in passing. Generic references such as 'a problem', 'some code' or 'an assignment' with nothing pinning them to something real don't count.

rubric.title: All four parts are illustrated with that task
rubric.description: Student gives an example for each of the four parts, drawn from the task they named rather than restating the definitions. Be generous about how thin or informally worded an example is - a short phrase pointing at something real counts, even if imperfectly explained. Deny only if an example is just the definition repeated in different words with nothing concrete added, or if most of the four have no real example attached at all.

rubric.title: The abstraction example names something deliberately ignored
rubric.description: Abstraction is the part beginners most often get wrong by describing simplification in general. Looking for: one specific detail they left out and why it did not matter - for example 'it does not matter what brand of bread it is'. Be generous about how it is worded; any gesture at something deliberately ignored counts. But do NOT credit an answer that describes choosing what to work on rather than what to leave out - 'I ignored the parts of the code that weren't broken' is focus, not abstraction, and calling it abstraction teaches the wrong idea. Say plainly that it is a different thing and point at the reading.

1-5-7-instructions-for-a-robot.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.5.5 (The Three As) and the worked example in 1.5.6 (The Jam Sandwich Robot): go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words are fine.

A robot is going to follow your instructions exactly. It knows nothing, it cannot guess, and it will not ask you a question.

1. Pick an everyday task: making a jam sandwich, tying a shoelace, brushing your teeth, feeding a pet. Name it, then write at least five numbered instructions for the robot.

2. Now read your own list back as if you were the robot, taking every word completely literally. Which instruction breaks first, and what exactly does the robot not know? (1.5.6)

3. Rewrite that one broken instruction so it works. It will probably become more than one instruction. (1.5.6)

4. In one or two sentences: why did you not notice the gap when you first wrote the list? (1.5.2)

rubric.title: A task is named and at least five numbered instructions are given
rubric.description: Student names one specific everyday task and writes five or more instructions as a numbered or clearly ordered list. Be generous about what counts as a task name and an instruction - informal phrasing is fine. If there are four solid instructions instead of five, credit as partial rather than missing; only fully withhold if the task isn't named at all or the list is clearly too short (two or three items).

rubric.title: Identifies a specific instruction that breaks
rubric.description: Student points at one of their own instructions and says it fails when read literally. Be generous about how specifically it's pointed at - referencing it by number, quoting it, or clearly describing which step it is all count. Only withhold credit if the answer stays at the level of a general observation ('the robot might get confused') with no particular instruction identifiable.

rubric.title: Names the unstated knowledge the robot lacks
rubric.description: Student says what the instruction assumed the reader already knew - where an object is, which hand to use, that a lid must be removed first, which side is up. Credit any concrete missing assumption, worded however roughly. Only withhold credit for answers that stay fully vague, like 'it is not clear enough' or 'the robot would be confused', with no actual assumption named.

rubric.title: The rewritten instruction actually closes the gap
rubric.description: The rewrite supplies the missing knowledge, and would survive being read literally. Be generous about how completely it closes the gap - it doesn't need to anticipate every possible literal reading, just the specific one identified in the prior step. Credit a rewrite that expands into several steps; that's the expected outcome. Only withhold credit if the rewrite doesn't actually add the missing information and just repeats the same assumption in different words - crediting that would tell the student they closed a gap that's still open.

rubric.title: Q4: explains why the gap was invisible at first
rubric.description: Student recognises that they were reading their own list with their own knowledge filled in - they knew what they meant, so the instruction looked complete. Be generous about how this is expressed; it doesn't need the course vocabulary, just the idea that their own familiarity hid the gap. Only withhold credit for answers like 'I was careless' or 'I rushed' that don't gesture at assumed knowledge at all.

1-6-3-ch1-pa-demo.prompt:
Both partners write this together and both submit the same answer. Everything asked for is something you did in the last hour or read earlier in Chapter 1; go back and reread if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout.

Part 1 -- Who did what. Name both partners. Then say who drove the keyboard for the chart (1.6.1), who drove it for the code (1.6.2), and one thing the partner who was not typing caught that the one typing had missed.

Part 2 -- Three test cases. A table or three rows, each with the numbers you put in, what you expected to come out, and what actually came out. At least one of your three has to land on the other side of the comparison from the other two -- a test set that only ever proves one answer has not tested the decision (1.5.40). Worked example, if you are on Slice Economics: a $16.00 pizza cut into 8 slices is $2.00 a slice, which is at the limit and counts as a good deal; a $20.00 pizza cut into 8 is $2.50 a slice, which is not. Those two land on opposite sides, which is what is being asked for. Three pizzas that all come out under $2.00 is what does not count, however different the numbers look.

Part 3 -- One thing you logged. Name one console.log you added while building that was there to check your work rather than to report the answer: what you printed, what it showed you, and what you changed because of it (1.5.41). If nothing was wrong, say what the print confirmed and how you would have known if it had been.

Part 4 -- Lifecycle. Chapter 1 opened with the four framework activities (1.1.6). They are:
  - inception -- the planning: deciding the goals and the overall scope
  - elaboration -- working out the requirements and designing the thing
  - construction -- writing and building it
  - deployment -- releasing it to the people who will use it
Pick ONE of those four for each third of this period -- the chart (1.6.1), the code (1.6.2), this writeup (1.6.3) -- and name it. Then say in one sentence why the chart came before the code rather than after.

Part 5 -- Paradigm and types. Two questions; answer both.
(a) Which paradigm is your program written in? Chapter 1 taught four. Pick ONE:
  - procedural -- a sequence of instructions carried out in order, with the data sitting in variables that the statements reach into from outside (1.4.8)
  - structured -- built only out of sequence, selection and repetition, with no jumping to an arbitrary line (1.4.9)
  - object-oriented -- data and the code that works on that data bundled together into objects (1.4.15)
  - functional -- built out of functions that take values in and hand values back, rather than changing things as they go (1.4.18)
Name the one your program is, then say in one sentence how you can TELL by looking at your own code. Point at something actually in your script.js, not at the definition.
(b) Your program produced two values that do not have the same type. typeof prints a type name for you (1.2.23), and the types Chapter 1 taught are number, string, boolean, undefined and null (1.2.27). Name the type of your computed value -- the cost per slice, the cost per person, the weighted average, or the tank range. Then name the type of your comparison -- the variable that stores the diamond (1.2.18). Then say in one sentence why those two are not the same type.

Part 6 -- The branch you did not write. Copy in the two pseudocode comment lines from your code, and say in one sentence what would have to be true before those comments could become real JavaScript.

rubric.title: Both partners named, with who drove which third
rubric.description: Two names appear, and the response says who had the keyboard for the chart and who had it for the code. Credit generously -- any clear division counts, including 'we swapped every ten minutes' as long as both names are there and both thirds are accounted for. The catch-something-missed detail is a bonus; do not withhold the criterion for a thin one. Withhold only if fewer than two names appear, or if the division of work is not stated at all.

rubric.title: Three test cases, with one landing on the other side of the comparison
rubric.description: Three sets of inputs are given, each with an expected result and an actual result. Credit rough tables, bullet lists or prose equally -- format is not being assessed. The one thing that matters: at least one case has to come out on the opposite side of the comparison from the others, so that both answers of the decision are exercised. Credit that if the response makes it visible in any way, including just saying 'this one was not a good deal'. If all three land on the same side, credit the criterion as partial and say why in the feedback.

rubric.title: One console.log used to check work, with what it showed
rubric.description: The response names one specific thing they printed while building, what it showed, and what they did next. Credit a print that confirmed something was already right just as fully as one that found a bug -- the response is allowed to say nothing was wrong, as long as it says what the print told them. Withhold only if no specific printed value is named at all, or the answer is generic advice about debugging rather than something that happened.

rubric.title: Each third mapped onto a framework activity, and design-before-code justified
rubric.description: The response assigns a lifecycle activity to each of the three thirds. Placements are allowed to be arguable -- the chart as elaboration or as inception, the writeup as deployment or as construction, are all defensible, and this criterion is about the mapping being attempted and reasoned, not about matching an answer key. Credit any three placements with any reasoning. The design-before-code sentence has to say something about catching problems early or about agreeing before typing; credit any version of that idea.

rubric.title: Paradigm named, and the two types distinguished
rubric.description: The response names a paradigm and says how the code shows it. For a straight-line Chapter 1 script the right answers are procedural or structured; credit imperative too if a student reaches for it. Object-oriented and functional are now offered as choices in the prompt and are NOT correct here -- a program with no objects, no classes and no functions is neither. If one of those two is named, withhold the paradigm half and say which feature of their own code rules it out. Any short justification carries the correct answer: a list of steps, runs top to bottom, no objects or classes. Then the response has to say the computed value is a number and the comparison is a boolean, with some statement of why they differ. Credit "one is a calculation, one is a yes or no" as a full answer to the why. If the paradigm is named but the type answer is missing, or vice versa, treat as partial.

rubric.title: The two pseudocode branches, and what would make them code
rubric.description: The two IF/ELSE comment lines from their program appear, quoted or paraphrased. Then one sentence about what is still missing -- the expected answer is the if statement, which is Chapter 2. Credit any answer that points at conditionals, if/else, or 'we have not learned that syntax yet'. Withhold only if the branches do not appear at all.

1-7-2-ch1-individual-pa-own-words.lessonTitle: 1.7.2 Individual PA Part 2: In Your Own Words

rubric.title: Umbrella activities
rubric.description: Says what makes an activity an umbrella activity (it runs across the whole project, alongside the framework activities), names a real one, and says what skipping it would cost.

rubric.title: What is wrong with the snippet
rubric.description: Names two of the snippet's several real faults with real consequences for the next reader, at least one of them about the comments saying nothing rather than there being too few. There is more than one valid pair.

rubric.title: High-level against low-level
rubric.description: Distinguishes the two by distance from the hardware and gives one genuine reason to accept the harder language.

1-7-5-ch1-individual-pa-write-the-steps.lessonTitle: 1.7.5 Individual PA Part 5: Write the Steps
1-7-5-ch1-individual-pa-write-the-steps.prompt:
This is the design item on a closed-book chapter test, sat individually in class at the end of Chapter 1. The student picked ONE of three problems in Part 4 and charted it; here they write the pseudocode for the same problem. The three problems were:

  Backpack Check -- given the number of textbooks, the weight of one textbook and the student's own weight, work out what the backpack weighs and compare it against one tenth of the student's weight.
  Screen Time -- given the minutes of screen time used across seven days, work out the daily average and compare it against 120 minutes.
  Print Job -- given the number of pages and a cost of 8 cents a page, work out what the job costs and compare it against the $5.00 left in the print account.

Work out which problem they chose from what they wrote, and mark against that one. Do not penalise a student for choosing a different problem from the one you would have picked.

WHAT PSEUDOCODE IS HERE (1.5.19, 1.5.20). Plain language arranged like code. Two rules and no others: one instruction per line, and indentation shows what sits inside what. It is not any programming language and it cannot be run.

MARK IT ON THESE THINGS AND NOTHING ELSE:

  Inputs -- every value the problem hands them is fetched before it is used. A student who computes an average without ever getting the minutes has skipped an input.
  The computation -- the one value the problem is about is worked out in a line that says HOW, not just that it happens. 'set cost to pages times 0.08' counts; 'work out the cost' does not.
  The comparison -- the threshold is asked as a question and BOTH answers are written out. A branch with only the yes side has tested half the problem, which is the fault 1.5.22 and 1.5.26 warn about -- both exits of a diamond have to go somewhere.
  Indentation -- the lines belonging to each answer are indented under it, and lines that happen regardless are not. This is the rule most likely to be broken and it is worth marking strictly, because moving a line in or out describes a different program.
  Plain language -- English, one instruction per line. JavaScript syntax is not required and not rewarded; a student who writes real code has answered a different question, but do not mark them down for it if the logic is right and readable.

Do NOT require any particular wording, keyword or layout beyond the two rules. Do NOT require a variable-naming convention. Do NOT reward length.

This is a test. Report what the student wrote against each criterion. Do not coach, do not supply the missing line, and do not suggest what to try next.

rubric.title: Every input is fetched before it is used
rubric.description: Each value the problem supplies appears in an instruction of its own before anything depends on it.

rubric.title: The one value is worked out, and the line says how
rubric.description: The quantity the problem is about is computed in a line that names the arithmetic, not one that merely announces the result.

rubric.title: The comparison is asked, and both answers are written
rubric.description: The threshold appears as a question with both outcomes written out, not one branch alone.

rubric.title: Indentation carries the branches
rubric.description: Lines belonging to an answer are indented under it; lines that happen regardless are not indented.

rubric.title: Plain language, one instruction per line
rubric.description: Written in English rather than JavaScript, with no line doing two things at once.

2-2-12-a5-2-flowchart-decision.prompt:
Draw a flowchart for this algorithm:

1. Start.
2. Get the customer's age.
3. If the age is under 13, the ticket costs $8. Otherwise the ticket costs $14.
4. Print the ticket price.
5. End.

Use an oval for Start and for End, a rectangle for each task, and a diamond for the decision. Label both arrows leaving the diamond so a reader knows which answer goes which way.

rubric.title: Gets the age before deciding
rubric.description: A task or input shape that obtains the customer's age appears on the path between Start and the decision diamond. Credit any reasonable wording: 'get age', 'ask for age', 'input age', or even just 'age' labeled on an input step. If the diagram jumps straight from Start to the decision with no step that obtains the age, that is a real structural gap - the diamond has nothing to test - so do not credit it, but be generous about how the step itself is worded or drawn.

rubric.title: Diamond asks the right question
rubric.description: The decision diamond tests the customer's age against 13, for example 'age < 13', 'under 13?', 'age less than 13'. Accept an equivalent inverted test such as 'age >= 13' as long as the branches below it are consistent with the direction of the test. Be generous about exact phrasing or how the number is presented. If the condition tests a different number entirely or a different quantity than age, that is testing the wrong thing rather than just being imprecise about the right thing, so do not credit it.

rubric.title: Both prices appear on the correct branches
rubric.description: One branch out of the diamond leads to $8 and the other to $14, and the branch labels match the condition. If the diamond asks 'age < 13', the yes branch must reach $8 and the no branch $14; if it asks 'age >= 13', the mapping is reversed. Be generous about how the branches are labeled - 'yes'/'no', 'true'/'false', or the literal condition text all count. But a missing price, both branches carrying the same price, or prices swapped relative to the condition mean the algorithm itself is wrong rather than just messily drawn, so do not credit those.

rubric.title: Both branches lead onward to the End
rubric.description: Neither branch is a dead end: following either answer out of the diamond eventually reaches the End oval, whether the two paths rejoin at a shared 'print the price' step or each prints separately before ending. Any structure that gets both branches to the End counts - only withhold credit if a branch genuinely stops with nothing after it.

rubric.title: Shapes are used for what they mean
rubric.description: Ovals are used only for Start and End, the diamond is used only for the question, and rectangles (or input/output parallelograms) carry the actions. Small variation in exactly which action lands in which action-shaped box is fine. But if the question ends up drawn as a rectangle instead of a diamond, or an action is drawn as a diamond, the shapes are no longer carrying their meaning - which is the whole point of shape vocabulary - so do not credit that.

2-2-4-a5-1-algorithm-writeup.prompt:
Everything you need is in 2.2.2 (What Is an Algorithm?), 2.2.3 (Programs Implement Algorithms) and the worked example in 2.2.5: go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words throughout.

Part 1, In your own words, what is an algorithm? One or two sentences. (2.2.2 and 2.2.3)

Part 2: Write a precise, step-by-step algorithm in plain English, not code, for an everyday task you know well: making a sandwich, tying your shoes, logging into a website, anything. Number the steps. Someone who has never done the task should be able to follow your steps exactly and succeed, so be precise: do not skip steps, and do not assume the reader "just knows" something. (2.2.5)

rubric.title: Defines algorithm in own words
rubric.description: Defines an algorithm as a precise, ordered set of steps to accomplish a task, in the student's own words.

rubric.title: Part 2 uses numbered, ordered steps
rubric.description: Part 2 is a numbered/ordered list of steps in a sensible sequence.

rubric.title: Steps are precise and unambiguous
rubric.description: Steps are precise and unambiguous: no major skipped step or 'and then it's done' hand-wave a beginner couldn't follow.

rubric.title: Steps complete the task from start to finish
rubric.description: The steps, followed exactly, actually accomplish the chosen task from start to finish.

2-3-27-written-justify-choice.lessonTitle: 2.3.27 switch or if...else? Justify Your Choice
2-3-27-written-justify-choice.prompt:
Answer all three, numbered Q1 to Q3. Everything you need is in 2.3.23 (Choosing Between if...else and switch) and the worked examples in 2.3.24 and 2.3.25: go back and reread them if you get stuck. A few sentences each is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Q1: A program routes a support ticket by its priority, which is always one of 'low', 'medium', or 'high'. Which statement fits better, switch or if...else? Explain why, in terms of what is being compared. (2.3.23, and the worked example in 2.3.24)

Q2: The grade chain from this section (score >= 90 prints A, score >= 80 prints B, and so on) cannot be rewritten as a switch. Explain why, in your own words. (2.3.23, and the worked example in 2.3.25)

Q3: Describe one program of your own choosing, real or made up, that could use either a switch or an if...else chain. Say which one you would pick and how you decided, using the same test from the reading. (2.3.23)

rubric.title: Q1: Picks switch and explains why
rubric.description: Answer picks switch and gives some real reason grounded in the finite-list idea - that priority is compared against a small set of exact values ('low', 'medium', 'high'), that there's no range or comparison involved, or something in that spirit even loosely worded. Deny if the answer picks if...else, or picks switch with no reasoning at all (a bare 'switch is better' with nothing behind it).

rubric.title: Q2: Explains why the grade chain can't become a switch
rubric.description: Answer explains that score >= 80 (and similar) is a range covering many values rather than one exact value, so it can't be written as a finite list of case values. Accept any phrasing that gestures at the range/boundary nature of the condition, even loosely - 'it's a range, not a specific number' is enough. Only deny a bare 'switch doesn't support >=' with nothing at all behind it.

rubric.title: Q3: Gives an own-choice example with a justified pick
rubric.description: Describes a concrete program scenario (not the priority or grade example already used), states which statement it would use, and gives some real reasoning behind the pick tied to the finite-list idea, however briefly. Deny if no reasoning at all is given, or if the example is just Q1/Q2 restated rather than something new.

3-1-7-a7-2-pass-by-reference-writeup.prompt:
Everything you need is in 3.6.1 (Pass by Value vs Reference) and 3.6.2 (Defensive Copying): go back and reread them if you get stuck. One or two sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

1. What does "pass by value" mean, and which kinds of values does JavaScript pass this way? (3.6.1)

2. What does "pass by reference" mean, and which kinds of values does JavaScript pass this way? (3.6.1)

3. Give one short example of each. You may describe the code in words rather than writing it. (3.6.1)

4. Why does this matter? Describe one bug that could happen if a programmer forgets the difference. (3.6.2)

rubric.title: Pass by value explained correctly
rubric.description: Explains pass-by-value: the function gets a copy; changes inside don't affect the original. Correctly says primitives (number/string/boolean) are passed by value.

rubric.title: Pass by reference explained correctly
rubric.description: Explains pass-by-reference: the function shares the same object/array; changes inside DO affect the original. Correctly says objects/arrays are passed by reference.

rubric.title: One example of each
rubric.description: Gives a plausible example of each (e.g., changing a number param has no outside effect; pushing to an array param does).

rubric.title: Describes a real consequence
rubric.description: Describes a real consequence: an unintended-mutation bug, or why you'd copy before changing.

4-1-5-q1-reflection-writeup.prompt:
This one is about your own work, so most of it comes from you rather than from a reading. 4.1.2 (Plan Before You Code) and 4.1.4 (Manual Testing) will help with question 2, and 1.1.6 (The Four Phases) is where the life-cycle phases were introduced. A few sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

1. Name one concept from this quarter: variables, conditionals, loops, functions, arrays, anything: that you found hardest, and explain how you worked through it.

2. Think about how you would build a small program now. Describe how you would plan it, build it, and test it, and connect that to the software-development life-cycle phases from Week 1. (4.1.2, 4.1.4 and 1.1.6)

3. What is one thing you want to get better at next quarter?

rubric.title: Names a hard concept and describes how they worked through it
rubric.description: Student names a specific Q1 concept they found hard (e.g., 'loops', 'functions', 'arrays') and names something they actually did about it, however briefly described - re-doing a problem a different way, asking someone, looking something up, working through an example by hand. Credit any real action, even a single sentence and even informally worded; 'I wrote the same loop five different ways' counts, and so does something similarly small. Deny only a fully generic 'I practiced' / 'I kept coding until it clicked' with no actual action behind it.

rubric.title: Describes a plan → build → test process for a small program
rubric.description: Student touches on planning, building, and testing a small program, in that order or a clearly recognizable sequence, however briefly each is mentioned - a single phrase for a stage is enough. Deny only if a whole stage is missing entirely, e.g. jumping straight to describing code with no mention of planning first or checking it works after.

rubric.title: Connects reflection to SDLC phases or lived experience this quarter
rubric.description: Student connects their plan/build/test description (Q2) to the SDLC phases from Week 1, or points to a specific moment from this quarter that illustrates one of those phases - even a loose or informally-worded connection counts, it doesn't need to name the phase precisely. Deny only a generic 'I know SDLC' or similar with no specific connection attached at all.

5-1-22-a10-2-frame-loop.prompt:
Answer all three. Everything you need is in 5.1.3 (Frame loop), 5.1.15 (Velocity) and the 5.1.12 video: go back and reread or rewatch if you get stuck. A few sentences each is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Question 1, In your own words, what is the difference between setup() and draw() in a moSHion sketch? When does each one run? (5.1.3, the worked example in 5.1.4, and the 5.1.12 video)

Question 2: moSHion runs at about 60 frames per second. If you set player.vel.x = 4, how many pixels does the sprite move in one second? Show your math. How far in 5 seconds? If your canvas is 400 pixels wide, roughly how long until the sprite crosses the whole canvas? (5.1.15)

Question 3: Why do you think the engine gives us vel (velocity) instead of making us set pos.x ourselves every frame? Give one reason. (5.1.15 and 5.1.16)

rubric.title: Q1: setup() vs draw() explained in your own words
rubric.description: Student clearly states setup() runs once at start and draw() runs every frame (about 60 times/sec). Bonus for mentioning setup() builds the world and draw() handles per-frame updates.

rubric.title: Q2: 60 fps math shown: 1-second and 5-second distances, canvas-crossing time
rubric.description: 4 px/frame × 60 fps = 240 px/sec. 5 sec = 1200 px. 400 px canvas / 240 px/sec ≈ 1.67 sec. Student must show at least one multiplication step, not just final numbers.

rubric.title: Q3: One sensible reason for using velocity instead of direct position
rubric.description: Any reasonable answer: lets physics/collisions integrate, smoother motion, avoids fighting the engine, frame-rate independence, etc. Looking for ONE clear reason: doesn't need to be the textbook answer.

5-3-32-a12-2-oop-writeup.prompt:
Answer all four questions. Questions 1 and 4 come from the readings; questions 2 and 3 come from code you have written yourself. Your own everyday words throughout: do not copy definitions from the internet.

Question 1: Definitions in your own words. What does procedural programming mean? What does object-oriented programming mean? (5.3.3, 5.4.14, and the side-by-side worked example in 5.4.15)

Question 2: A specific procedural example from Q1. Name a specific assignment or program you wrote in Q1 that used a procedural approach, and describe it in one or two sentences. Name the assignment.

Question 3: A specific moSHion OOP example. Name a specific place in your moSHion code: the A12.1 Collectible class, or an earlier class you wrote: where you used OOP. Describe how the class organised your code: what data and what behaviour did it group together? (5.3.7 and 5.4.1)

Question 4: When OOP wins. Describe one situation, hypothetical is fine, where OOP is clearly the better choice than procedural code. Explain why, using at least one of these: readability, extensibility, or keeping data and behaviour together. (5.4.16 and 5.4.17)

rubric.title: Q1: Both terms defined in own words
rubric.description: Student defines procedural programming (code as a sequence of instructions, top-to-bottom or function-based flow) AND OOP (organizing code into classes/objects that bundle data and behavior), in their own words even if informal or imprecise. Credit any answer that gestures at both ideas in the right direction, even loosely worded - it doesn't need textbook precision. Deny only if a definition is missing entirely or is copied rather than in the student's own words.

rubric.title: Q2: Specific Q1 procedural example named
rubric.description: Student names a specific Q1 assignment (by name or description) and says something, however brief, about how it used a procedural approach. Any real named assignment with even a loose description counts - it doesn't need to be precise or detailed. Deny only a fully generic statement like 'I used procedural code in Q1' with nothing pinning it to an actual assignment, or no example at all.

rubric.title: Q3: Specific moSHion OOP example named
rubric.description: Student names a specific class from their moSHion code (e.g., Collectible, Player, Enemy) and says something, however brief, about how it organized their code - what it held, or how it cut down repetition. Any real named class with even a loose explanation counts. Deny only a generic reference to 'using a class' with nothing specific named, or no example at all.

rubric.title: Q4: OOP-wins scenario with reasoning
rubric.description: Student describes a scenario (real or hypothetical) where OOP is the better approach and gives some reason why - readability (easier to understand), extensibility (easy to add more objects/types), or separation of data and behaviour (the object owns its own state). One reason is enough, and it counts however loosely it is worded; a student who says 'it would be easier to add more enemies later' has given the extensibility reason. Credit a scenario with any real reason attached. A scenario with no reason at all is partial. Reserve missing for a response with no scenario.

rubric.title: Writing clarity
rubric.description: Response is clearly organized and easy to follow. Deduct this point only for significant issues: incoherent structure, or writing that makes it difficult to assess the content. Do not deduct for length.

7-1-2-q2-reflection.prompt:
This one is entirely about the game you built, so there is no reading to look up: the answers come from your own project and your own memory of building it. A few sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words. There is no wrong answer here as long as you are describing your actual project honestly.

1. Your game changed between the pitch in your README and the version you handed in. Name one thing that changed, and explain what made you change it.

2. Describe one bug that took you more than a few minutes to find. How did you track it down?

3. The checklist gave you twelve requirements and no design. Which requirement was hardest to fit into YOUR game idea, and what did you do about it?

rubric.title: Names a specific change from pitch to shipped, and what caused it
rubric.description: Student names something concrete that differs between their README pitch and the game they handed in, with some reason behind it, however brief - playtesting, scope, something that wasn't fun or didn't work. A short, real, named change with a one-phrase reason counts; 'the enemies chased the player and it was impossible, so I made them patrol instead' is the clean case, but a thinner version of the same shape still counts. Deny only fully generic non-answers like 'I changed some stuff' or 'I added more features' that don't name anything real.

rubric.title: Gives a real account of tracking down one bug
rubric.description: Student describes a specific bug and something about how they tracked it down, however briefly - printing values, commenting code out, reading an error, checking one thing at a time. A short, real account counts even if thin; deny only a response that names a bug but skips the hunt entirely ('my sprite wouldn't move, then I fixed it'), or a bug so vague a reader couldn't picture it at all.

rubric.title: Explains fitting a required feature into their own design
rubric.description: Student identifies which checklist requirement was hardest to justify inside their particular game and says something about the decision they made - reworking the design to need it, or finding a use that fits - however briefly. This is about design judgment, not difficulty of coding, so 'joints were hard to code' still doesn't earn it, but a thinner version of 'my game had nothing to save so I added a high score table' does.
